title: Can one person attend every meeting
prompt:
Given meetings as [start, end) pairs, return true if one person could attend all of them, meaning no two meetings overlap.

- 0 to 100,000 meetings in any order, with integers 0 <= start < end <= 10^9.
- end is exclusive: [1, 3] and [3, 5] do not conflict, but [1, 3] and [2, 5] do.
- An empty list returns true.
hints: Comparing every pair works but is O(n²). Which meetings are the only candidates to clash with a given one?
Sort the meetings by start time. Then a meeting can only clash with the one just before it.
After sorting, return false as soon as some start is strictly less than the previous meeting's end.

solution.explanation: Once meetings are sorted by start, if any two overlap then some adjacent pair overlaps too, because a meeting that overlaps a later one also overlaps everything starting between them. So a single comparison of each start with the previous end is enough.

complexity.notes: Sorting dominates. Space is for the sorted copy; sorting in place would avoid it at the cost of mutating the input.

followUps: If conflicts exist, how many rooms would be needed to hold every meeting?
